title: DDIA 1 · RELIABLE, SCALABLE, MAINTAINABLE
subtitle: The three words every NFR discussion comes back to.
footer: Study notes on Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann). Read the book.

blocks.text: A failure is when the whole system stops serving users. You design so faults don't become failures.
Reads become one cache lookup. The cost moved to write time.
The user waits for the slowest backend. With 100 backends at 1% slow each, 63% of user requests hit at least one slow call.

panels.label: SCALING UP VS SCALING OUT, AND

head: Choice
What it means
When it wins
rows: Bigger machine: more cores, RAM, NVMe
Simple, no distribution bugs. A single Postgres box handles 10–50k TPS. Start here.
When one box is not enough or you need fault tolerance.
Unpredictable load. Manual scaling is simpler and has fewer surprises.
Easy for ops to keep running
Monitoring, good defaults, predictable behaviour, runbooks.
Good abstractions, for example SQL hiding storage and concurrency.

blocks.text: There is no "magic scaling sauce". An architecture for 100k req/sec of 1KB reads looks nothing like one for 3 req/min of 2GB uploads.

items: Name the load parameter (reads/sec, fan-out, data size), calculate it, then say which component breaks first.
p99 < 200ms for reads, not averages. Mention tail amplification if requests fan out.
Separate fault from failure: "A node dying is a fault. Replicas plus health checks mean it never becomes a failure."

blocks.text: "Before choosing components, let me pin down the load parameters: DAU, read:write ratio, and peak QPS, because they decide whether we need any distribution at all."
